paragraphs: A Markov random field describes variables whose choices interact through a graph. Finding the configuration with the lowest energy becomes difficult when that graph contains cycles. One strategy for larger problems is to split them into simpler pieces. Cycle-shaped pieces can give a tighter approximation than tree-shaped pieces, but solving those cycles can become the computational bottleneck.

The paper develops a fast algorithm that solves energy minimization exactly when the graph is a cycle. It builds on junction-tree message passing, where intermediate tables communicate information about possible assignments. The speedup comes from pruning many entries in those tables using conditions that exploit the cycle structure, while preserving an exact solution.

Experiments report speeds more than an order of magnitude faster than other leading fast inference methods, with consistent performance across several real problems. The practical contribution is an efficient cycle solver that can serve inside algorithms for general graphs. Exactness applies to the cycle subproblem; its role in larger problems is as a useful computational building block.
icml-2013-a-fast-and-exact-energy-minimi.tldr: An exact cycle-MRF solver accelerates message passing by pruning entries according to the graph’s cycle structure.

paragraphs: Finding a useful cluster in a huge graph need not require processing the entire graph. This paper studies local algorithms based on random walks, with running time tied to the size of the cluster they return. That computational goal makes the approach relevant when the desired output is small relative to the surrounding network.

The authors develop a method with stronger theoretical guarantees for both clustering accuracy and the conductance of the returned set. Conductance describes how strongly a set connects outward relative to its size in the graph. The improvement is especially associated with clusters that are well connected internally: stronger internal connectivity leads to a more substantial advantage over previous work.

The paper also proves that its analysis is tight and evaluates the method on synthetic and real data. These results help explain why some random-walk methods can work better in practice than earlier theory suggested. The central insight is that internal connectivity provides useful structure for analyzing local clustering, beyond simply asking whether a cluster has few outward connections.
icml-2013-a-local-algorithm-for-finding-.tldr: A local random-walk clustering method gains stronger guarantees when the desired cluster is well connected internally.

paragraphs: Separating a single audio recording into its component sources is useful for denoising, transcription, remixing, and audio analysis. Models based on non-negative matrix factorization can perform this separation, but the abstract identifies two practical problems: weak results without isolated training examples and limited ability for users to correct an unsatisfactory decomposition.

The proposed system lets a user paint annotations on a display showing how sound varies across time and frequency. Those annotations guide a latent variable model through posterior regularization. Specifically, they impose linear grouping constraints on the model’s inferred explanation of the recording, expressing relationships that would be difficult to impose through standard prior distributions.

For the constraints studied, the authors derive an efficient expectation-maximization algorithm with closed-form multiplicative updates. This connects the method to existing matrix-factorization techniques while supporting interactive computation. The stated result is high-quality separation at interactive rates without explicit training data. Human feedback becomes part of the learning process, allowing the decomposition to respond directly to annotations on the sound itself.
icml-2013-an-efficient-posterior-regular.tldr: User annotations on a time-frequency display guide efficient sound-source separation without explicit training data.

paragraphs: When training and testing data follow different distributions, a classifier may struggle to transfer what it has learned. A common response is to make the training distribution resemble the test distribution. This paper argues that, for kernel methods, the relevant comparison should account for the feature space created by the kernel, because its geometry directly affects learning.

The authors propose matching distributions in that Hilbert space. Given a predefined empirical kernel map, the task becomes one of aligning kernel matrices across domains. These matrices describe relationships among samples, but comparing them is challenging when they are defined over different sample collections. The paper introduces surrogate kernels, based on Mercer’s theorem, to evaluate their similarity.

This approach connects adaptation to the representation actually used by the kernel learner. Its significance is the choice of where distribution matching occurs and how otherwise differently indexed kernel matrices can be compared. The abstract reports promising results on several real-world applications, supporting the usefulness of adapting to kernel-space geometry in the settings examined.
icml-2013-covariate-shift-in-hilbert-spa.tldr: Surrogate kernels enable distribution matching in the feature space used by kernel learners under covariate shift.

paragraphs: Compressed sensing often treats the number of nonzero signal entries as known, although that quantity is usually unavailable in practice. Exact counting is also unstable: tiny nonzero entries count just as much as large ones. The paper therefore estimates an effective sparsity measure, defined as the squared L1 norm divided by the squared L2 norm.

This measure is a sharp lower bound on the number of nonzero coordinates and provides a more stable description of how spread out a signal is. The proposed estimator uses a small number of linear measurements, requires little computation, and does not assume the signal is sparse. Its confidence interval has a width that does not depend on the signal’s dimension.

The framework also extends to estimating a soft version of matrix rank with analogous guarantees. A further theoretical result explains the role of randomness: when measurements are far fewer than coordinates, deterministic measurements have large minimax estimation risk. Thus the paper combines a practical uncertainty-aware estimator with a specific justification for randomized measurement design.
icml-2013-estimating-unknown-sparsity-in.tldr: A lightweight randomized estimator measures effective signal sparsity with confidence-interval width independent of signal dimension.

paragraphs: Kernel methods depend on expressive nonlinear function classes, but computing the representations needed to use them can be expensive. Fastfood addresses this computational burden by improving random kitchen sinks, an approach for constructing randomized feature expansions. The aim is to make nonlinear estimation substantially cheaper while preserving the accuracy of the approximation.

The proposed computation runs in log-linear time. The paper also connects representation design to regularization: changing the spectral distribution of the projection matrix changes the kernel’s regularization properties. This means the construction offers a way to adjust how the kernel constrains the functions it learns, alongside its computational benefits.

Experiments report two orders of magnitude faster computation and three orders of magnitude less memory use, with gains already appearing on moderately small problems. These are reported experimental improvements, while the abstract separately states that the faster construction does not sacrifice accuracy. Together, the contributions make feature expansion more economical and provide a mechanism for controlling the resulting kernel’s regularization behavior.
icml-2013-fastfood-computing-hilbert-spa.tldr: Fastfood speeds randomized nonlinear feature expansions in log-linear time while reducing memory use and enabling control over kernel regularization.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate the parameters of a tree-shaped probabilistic model containing hidden variables. It treats the joint probability table of the observed variables as a tensor, or multidimensional array. Hidden variables create low-rank structure when that array is reshaped into different matrices, and those structures together imply a hierarchical tensor decomposition.

This perspective gives parameter estimation a shared optimization objective: minimize the Frobenius-norm difference between the probability tensor and its decomposition. When the latent tree model is correctly specified, the authors show that a recursive decomposition algorithm can reach a global optimum. Existing spectral algorithms for hidden Markov models and latent trees emerge as special cases, clarifying the objective behind them.

The framework also addresses model misspecification, where the chosen model does not correctly describe the data. For that case, the authors derive an improved decomposition and provide an approximation guarantee. Experiments on synthetic and real data report significant improvements over leading methods. The contribution therefore combines an explanation of established estimators with a new estimator for imperfectly specified models.
icml-2013-hierarchical-tensor-decomposit.tldr: A hierarchical tensor objective unifies latent-tree estimators and yields an improved estimator for misspecified models.

paragraphs: Transfer learning and active learning address limited labels in complementary ways. Transfer learning borrows information from a related labeled source, while active learning selects examples for people to label. The paper brings these decisions together, arguing through its formulation that the usefulness of source data and the choice of target examples can be assessed jointly.

The proposed framework solves one convex optimization problem that simultaneously weights source-domain examples and selects a batch of target-domain examples for annotation. Both decisions serve a common objective: reduce the distribution difference between the combined reweighted source and queried target data, and the remaining unlabeled target data. Thus annotation choices and source weighting are coordinated through the same distribution-matching goal.

Experiments on three real-world datasets report classification accuracy improvements of 5% to 10% over an existing two-stage approach. The findings support the value of integrating the two learning procedures in the evaluated settings. The methodological contribution is a single optimization framework that decides which existing labels to emphasize while also deciding which new labels to request.
icml-2013-joint-transfer-and-batch-mode-.tldr: A single convex objective jointly weights labeled source data and selects target examples for annotation.

paragraphs: This paper approaches fair classification by changing the representation of the data before making predictions. It addresses two notions of fairness: group fairness, where a protected group receives positive classifications at the population-wide rate, and individual fairness, where similar people receive similar treatment. The proposed algorithm is presented as achieving both forms of fairness.

Learning the representation involves competing objectives. It should preserve useful information about the original data while obscuring information about protected-group membership. Framing this tension as an optimization problem makes the representation itself a central part of the fairness mechanism. The task is to retain information needed for classification while reducing what the representation reveals about the protected attribute.

The authors report positive results against other known techniques on three datasets. They also show that the intermediate representation can support other classification tasks, making transfer learning possible. A further contribution is progress toward learning a distance metric that identifies dimensions relevant to classification. These findings connect fairness-aware representation learning with reuse across tasks and the question of how individual similarity should be measured.
icml-2013-learning-fair-representations-.tldr: The paper learns representations that preserve useful data information while obscuring protected-group membership to support fair classification.

paragraphs: Lists produced by people contain dependencies between entries, so treating every item as an independent draw can miss important structure. This paper introduces sampling with reduced replacement, called SWIRL, as a generative model for such lists. It relates the model to standard sampling schemes and provides a maximum-likelihood method for fitting it to observed data.

One application concerns people who spontaneously suggest associations between text features and labels. These volunteered pairs provide information for text classification even when the contributors are not experts. Incorporating SWIRL improves the accuracy of leading feature-learning frameworks in this task, showing that modeling how suggestions are generated can make the resulting supervision more useful.

The second application concerns verbal fluency: people generate words after receiving a category prompt. For lists from healthy participants and patients with brain damage, the learned parameters align well with existing psychological theories. The model can also distinguish the two groups from their lists. Together, the applications show how the same account of dependent list generation can support both predictive learning and psychologically meaningful analysis.
icml-2013-learning-from-human-generated-.tldr: SWIRL models dependencies in human-generated lists, improving volunteered-feature learning and supporting analysis of verbal-fluency responses.

paragraphs: Sparse regression methods such as the Lasso and Dantzig selector need noise-variance information to tune their regularization appropriately. This becomes difficult when noise levels are unknown or vary with the observations. The paper targets this issue in high-dimensional regression and autoregression, where assuming a single known noise level can be an obstacle to using sparse estimation.

The proposed approach estimates the conditional mean and conditional variance together. These describe, respectively, the expected response and the amount of noise around that response under the observed conditions. Joint estimation addresses the need to learn the predictive relationship while also accounting for changing uncertainty, within the group-sparsity setting identified by the paper.

A central computational feature is that the estimator can be obtained by solving a second-order cone program, a convex optimization formulation. The authors state that this makes it efficiently computable even for very large problems. They provide theoretical analysis and numerical assessments of performance. The contribution is therefore a tractable joint estimation method for settings where noise information cannot readily be supplied in advance.
icml-2013-learning-heteroscedastic-model.tldr: A convex estimator jointly learns conditional means and changing noise variances in high-dimensional regression.

paragraphs: K-means can be understood through a limiting connection to Gaussian mixture models: as Gaussian covariances shrink toward zero, the likelihood objective and expectation-maximization procedure approach their K-means counterparts. This paper uses that connection as motivation for deriving simple optimization methods from richer Bayesian nonparametric models through small-variance asymptotics.

Its key choice is to apply the limiting argument directly to the posterior distribution. That makes the framework independent of a particular Bayesian inference algorithm and allows it to extend beyond Dirichlet-process mixtures. For feature learning, the authors apply it to models using beta-process and Indian-buffet-process priors, obtaining an objective that learns groupings while penalizing the introduction of new ones.

Those groupings relax clustering’s requirements that memberships be mutually exclusive and exhaustive. This broadens the kind of structure the resulting optimization can represent beyond assigning each item to exactly one cluster. The paper presents several algorithms described as scalable and simple to implement, and reports empirical benefits. Its broader contribution is a reusable route from Bayesian modeling choices to practical optimization objectives.
icml-2013-mad-bayes-map-based-asymptotic.tldr: MAD-Bayes derives simple, scalable optimization methods by applying small-variance limits directly to Bayesian nonparametric posteriors.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to combine several measured variables into a signal that strongly tends to return toward its mean. It searches over affine combinations, which allow weighted sums together with an offset. Alongside maximizing mean reversion, it requires the resulting signal’s variance to stay above a chosen threshold.

That variance constraint captures a practical tradeoff. A signal may show desirable mean-reverting behavior but fluctuate too little to be useful. In the financial application described by the authors, the goal is to identify mean-reverting portfolios with enough variation to overcome market friction. More generally, mean reversion and related properties serve as proxies for stationarity, while variance represents signal strength.

The authors study several formulations and show that many of the resulting optimization problems can be solved exactly through semidefinite programming and a variant of the S-lemma. The significance is computational: the search for combinations satisfying both temporal behavior and minimum strength can, in these cases, be handled by exact optimization methods. The stated exactness applies to many of the studied problems, rather than every possible formulation.
icml-2013-mean-reversion-with-a-variance.tldr: The paper finds strongly mean-reverting variable combinations with minimum variance, solving many formulations exactly through semidefinite programming.

paragraphs: Expectation propagation approximates Bayesian inference through efficient message passing. It can struggle when its chosen family of approximate distributions cannot closely represent the true posterior. In that situation, the approximation may be inaccurate and the iterative updates may diverge. This paper modifies the matching requirements used during those updates to address that mismatch.

The proposed method, relaxed expectation propagation, minimizes a divergence equipped with an L1 penalty. This adaptively relaxes the moment-matching condition used by standard expectation propagation. The central idea is to give the approximation procedure room to adjust how closely it enforces those statistical matches when working within a restricted distribution family.

For Gaussian process classification, experiments report significant improvements over expectation propagation and power expectation propagation in stability, estimation accuracy, and prediction. The authors also derive relaxed belief propagation as a special case for discrete Markov random fields. There, results show more accurate estimates than belief propagation and fractional belief propagation when interactions between nodes are strong. The evidence connects the relaxation to improvements in two distinct inference settings.
icml-2013-message-passing-with-l1-penali.tldr: An L1-penalized divergence relaxes message-passing moment matching, improving approximate inference in the evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Data can describe the same objects through several sources or types of features. Combining those views often involves assigning one weight to each source. This paper points out that such weighting can be too coarse: a feature’s usefulness may depend on which cluster of objects is being considered, even within a single source.

The proposed model integrates the features while learning a separate weight for each feature with respect to each cluster. New joint structured sparsity-inducing norms organize this selection and weighting process. This gives the model a way to represent different patterns of relevance across clusters. The framework also extends to classification when label information is available.

The authors derive an efficient algorithm for the optimization problem and prove its convergence. They evaluate the framework on five multi-view datasets for clustering and classification, reporting better performance than related leading methods throughout the experiments. The results support the value of finer-grained feature weighting in the tested settings, while the methodological contribution is a shared framework for learning which features matter to which groups.
icml-2013-multi-view-clustering-and-feat.tldr: Structured sparsity lets a multi-view model learn feature importance separately for each cluster and extend to classification.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent updates a model using noisy information from sampled data. Its performance depends heavily on the learning rates that control update size and on how those rates change during training. This paper proposes adjusting multiple learning rates automatically, with the objective of minimizing expected error at the current point in learning.

The method bases its adjustments on local variations in gradients across samples. Those variations provide information for choosing update sizes from the learning process itself. Rates are allowed to rise as well as fall, giving the procedure flexibility when the problem changes over time. The abstract identifies this property as making the approach suitable for non-stationary problems.

Across a collection of convex and non-convex tasks, the resulting algorithm matches the performance of the best settings found through systematic search. These experiments support the claim that the method effectively removes the need for learning-rate tuning in the evaluated tasks. The practical contribution is to replace that tuning effort with an adaptive rule driven by observed gradient behavior.
icml-2013-no-more-pesky-learning-rates-c.tldr: Gradient variation drives automatic learning-rate adjustments that match systematically tuned settings in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a model of possible transitions to plan better actions. A traditional planning update, called a full backup, combines current value estimates from successor states. Its computational cost therefore grows with the number of possible successors. This can make individual planning operations expensive when a state has many possible outcomes.

The paper introduces a small backup that uses the current value of just one successor state. The cost of this individual update does not depend on the total number of successors. Breaking planning into these smaller operations gives an algorithm finer control over how it spends computation, because it can update contributions at a more detailed level.

The authors implement prioritized sweeping using small backups and compare it empirically with classical implementations. They report a substantial performance improvement, supporting the claim that finer control can make planning more efficient. The key contribution is the planning operation itself: it creates a basis for a class of model-based methods that can allocate computational effort more flexibly.
icml-2013-planning-by-prioritized-sweepi.tldr: Small backups update planning values from one successor at a time, enabling more efficient prioritized sweeping in experiments.

paragraphs: When labeled training data are scarce, additional data can help, but familiar approaches impose restrictions on where those data come from. The abstract contrasts same-distribution unlabeled images in semi-supervised learning with labeled images from related homogeneous tasks in transfer learning. The proposed self-taught approach is designed to use unlabeled data without those source restrictions.

The method learns a dictionary using a robust loss function. Dictionary basis vectors provide components for representing examples, and structured sparse regularization selects useful components while incorporating supervision from the labeled data. This connects the representation learned from unlabeled examples to the distinctions relevant to the supervised task.

The authors derive an efficient iterative optimization algorithm and rigorously prove its convergence. Extensive experiments produce results described as promising. The contribution combines flexibility in the source of unlabeled data with a mechanism for selecting task-relevant dictionary elements. Its convergence result supports the optimization procedure, while the experimental results support the usefulness of the overall learning approach in the examined settings.
icml-2013-robust-and-discriminative-self.tldr: Robust dictionary learning and structured sparsity use unrestricted-source unlabeled data to build task-relevant representations.

paragraphs: Policy iteration repeatedly evaluates a decision policy and then tries to improve it. When either step is approximate, the resulting policies may fail to improve steadily and can oscillate. This paper studies how to choose the improvement step more carefully so that approximate computations do not simply lead to repeated, potentially unhelpful policy changes.

The authors define safe improvement through a lower bound on performance improvement relative to the current policy. At each iteration, the procedure searches for a policy that maximizes this bound. If it cannot find an improving policy, it stops. This makes a conservative assessment of improvement central to the update decision, rather than relying only on an estimated greedy policy.

Two algorithms implement this idea, differing in how they choose the next policy relative to that greedy estimate. The paper develops and discusses their theoretical basis, then evaluates them against leading approaches on chain-walk domains and Blackjack. The abstract identifies these comparisons without stating a particular winning result. The main contribution is the lower-bound-based framework for selecting and stopping policy improvements.
icml-2013-safe-policy-iteration-7004134c.tldr: Two policy-iteration algorithms choose updates by maximizing a lower bound on improvement and stop when no improving policy is found.

paragraphs: Sparse representations describe examples using a limited set of components from a learned dictionary. This paper develops a framework that combines kernel smoothing with marginal regression to learn such representations. Its aim is to incorporate relationships already present in the data while making the computation of sparse codes fast enough for large dictionaries.

Nonparametric kernel smoothing provides a flexible way to use feature similarity or temporal information. The authors also analyze generalization for dictionary learning under this smooth sparse-coding framework. Their bounds show how the required sample size depends on the L1 norm of the smoothing kernel, explicitly connecting a property of the chosen kernel to statistical learning requirements.

Marginal regression supplies the sparse codes and is reported to improve speed significantly, allowing the approach to scale readily to large dictionary sizes. Experiments on several real datasets demonstrate advantages in accuracy and speed. The paper also shows how the framework could improve semi-supervised sparse coding. Together, these contributions link structured information in the data, computational efficiency, and theoretical control over generalization.
icml-2013-smooth-sparse-coding-via-margi.tldr: Kernel smoothing incorporates data relationships into sparse coding, while marginal regression speeds code computation for large dictionaries.

paragraphs: Partially observable Markov decision processes model decisions when the underlying state is not directly known. Continuous state spaces create a major computational challenge because they contain infinitely many possibilities. The paper proposes learning a discrete representation of that space so that the integrals needed for planning can be computed efficiently and sparse calculations can generalize across the space.

The representation is refined iteratively within a new value-iteration step, without depending on prior knowledge for its construction. A self-correction algorithm is used to establish consistency of the learned generalization. This makes the representation part of the evolving planning procedure, allowing it to be improved as value iteration proceeds.

The implementation supports continuous state and observation spaces through Monte Carlo approximation and is designed to accommodate arbitrary POMDP models. In the reported experimental comparison, it obtains higher values in significantly less time than leading algorithms and solves higher-dimensional problems. The contribution is an integrated approach to learning the space representation and performing planning, with empirical gains from using that representation to organize continuous computations.
icml-2013-solving-continuous-pomdps-valu.tldr: A continuously refined discrete representation makes value iteration more efficient for continuous-state and continuous-observation POMDPs.

paragraphs: Neighborhood Components Analysis learns a distance measure for nearest-neighbor classification, but its model selects only one neighbor per point. That aligns naturally with a classifier using one neighbor, even though using several neighbors is often preferred for robustness. The paper introduces kNCA to learn distances suited to a classifier with an arbitrary neighborhood size.

The main technical result is an efficient way to compute and optimize the expected classification accuracy of that multi-neighbor classifier. This aligns the learning objective with the neighborhood size used for prediction. The authors also extend the same ideas to unsupervised embedding, producing kSNE and ktSNE as neighborhood-based generalizations of SNE and tSNE.

Neighborhood size becomes a control over the embedding, allowing more homogeneous and interpretable regions. Experiments show that kNCA often improves classification accuracy over leading methods and is more robust to label noise. They also reveal qualitative embedding changes as the neighborhood size varies. These findings support treating neighborhood size as part of the learned representation’s design, with consequences for both prediction and visualization.
icml-2013-stochastic-k-neighborhood-sele.tldr: kNCA learns distances for arbitrary-size nearest-neighbor classifiers, with related extensions offering neighborhood-size control over embeddings.

paragraphs: Bayesian networks can describe how data are generated as well as support classification. Training them primarily to separate classes often improves predictions but weakens their generative interpretation. This paper proposes a hybrid training method intended to obtain strong classification while retaining part of the model’s ability to explain the observed data probabilistically.

The method uses a large-margin formulation similar to a support vector machine, with a likelihood-weighted L1 penalty. This construction simultaneously optimizes data likelihood, helping preserve the model’s generative character. For many network structures, the objective can be formulated as a convex problem, which guarantees a globally optimal solution in those cases.

The reported models outperform leading generative and discriminative Bayesian-network training methods in classification and perform comparably to linear and kernelized support vector machines. They also achieve likelihoods close to the maximum-likelihood solution and behave robustly in classification experiments with missing features. These results support the proposed compromise: discriminative performance can improve while substantial generative quality remains, rather than being entirely sacrificed during training.
icml-2013-the-most-generative-maximum-ma.tldr: Likelihood-weighted large-margin training improves Bayesian-network classification while partly preserving generative quality.

paragraphs: Bayesian decision-tree learning places a prior over possible trees and updates it using data to obtain a posterior distribution. Existing Bayesian approaches commonly approximate that distribution by repeatedly modifying complete trees through Monte Carlo steps. This differs from familiar decision-tree algorithms that build a tree from the top down.

The paper introduces a sequential Monte Carlo algorithm that also proceeds from the top down. Its construction follows the broad behavior of classic tree-building methods while retaining the Bayesian goal of posterior inference. The change addresses the computational route used to explore trees, seeking the speed of top-down construction within a probabilistic learning framework.

Experiments show accuracy comparable to the most popular Markov chain Monte Carlo method while running more than an order of magnitude faster. This establishes a better computation–accuracy tradeoff in the reported evaluation. The result matters because competitive Bayesian tree prediction need not require the same expense as iteratively revising complete trees; sequential construction offers an empirically effective alternative.
icml-2013-top-down-particle-filtering-fo.tldr: Top-down sequential Monte Carlo makes Bayesian decision-tree inference over an order of magnitude faster in experiments while retaining comparable accuracy.

paragraphs: Learning a latent tree means discovering how observed variables are connected through hidden ones. Many existing approaches require the number of hidden states to be supplied beforehand, even though that number is itself unknown. This paper develops a structure-learning method that does not need that input, using relationships among groups of four observed variables.

For each quartet, the authors study the tensor representing its marginal probability distribution. A new characterization of tensor rank supports a nuclear-norm-based test for deciding the quartet’s relationship within the tree. This local test becomes a subroutine in a divide-and-conquer algorithm that reconstructs the larger latent structure.

Under mild conditions, the algorithm is consistent, and its error probability decreases exponentially as the sample size grows. The paper also reports favorable comparisons with alternatives. On a real stock dataset, it discovers meaningful variable groupings and yields a better-fitting model. The contribution connects a local algebraic test to global structure recovery, with conditional theoretical guarantees and empirical evidence for its usefulness.
icml-2013-unfolding-latent-tree-structur.tldr: Quartet tensor tests recover latent-tree structure without requiring the number of hidden states in advance.
